name: The Pomiserania Lodge & Motel
description: During Idlewild’s years as one of America’s most important Black resort communities, the Pomiserania Lodge provided lodging and meals for travelers who came to experience Black Eden. The property appeared in editions of The Negro Travelers’ Green Book, documenting its place within the network of businesses that welcomed Black travelers during segregation.
photo_notes: Likely available through Idlewild/Lake County archives; no clearly identified public photograph confirmed yet.

name: Lydia Inn & Castallante Pizza
description: Lydia Inn was one of Idlewild’s early lodging establishments. A 1959 account described it as one of the first three places in the community to accommodate guests, remembering generations of founders and visitors who came to Black Eden. Its later uses illustrate how Idlewild’s historic buildings continued serving the community across generations.
photo_notes: Historical Lydia Inn imagery is likely available in local collections; current building photos may also be available.

name: Sweetheart Motel
description: Once one of Idlewild’s most popular motels, the eleven-unit Sweetheart welcomed visitors and performers during the 1950s and 1960s. Entertainers including Joe “Ziggy” Johnson stayed here while working Idlewild’s celebrated entertainment circuit. Its surviving structure offers an opportunity to show how historic places can be adapted for new generations.
photo_notes: Documented in preservation materials and contemporary records.

name: Holiday House
description: The Holiday House is part of the story of Paradise Gardens, the district developed by pioneering Idlewild entrepreneurs Herman and Lela Wilson. The Wilsons helped transform the Paradise Lake area into a center for lodging, business and nightlife. Later stewardship by the Lindsey family represents the multigenerational care that has helped preserve Idlewild’s places and stories.
photo_notes: Present-day photos are findable; historical images may be in local archives.

name: Yates School #3 / Idlewild Public Library / Township Hall
description: This site reflects the everyday institutions that sustained Idlewild beyond its famous clubs and hotels. Education, local government and access to books and information were essential parts of community life, making this area an important reminder that Black Eden was not simply a vacation destination — it was a living community.
photo_notes: Likely available, especially library and township-related images.

name: Paradise Lake
description: Paradise Lake became the setting for one of Idlewild’s most important business and entertainment districts. Herman and Lela Wilson developed Paradise Gardens nearby, creating lodging, commercial spaces and the legendary Paradise Club. The lake remains part of the natural landscape that made Idlewild both a retreat and a place where Black entrepreneurship could flourish.
photo_notes: Both historic and contemporary lake photographs are readily documented.

name: Lake Idlewild
description: At the heart of Black Eden, Lake Idlewild offered generations of residents and visitors space to swim, boat, gather and relax. Along its shoreline grew cottages, businesses and social institutions that helped make Idlewild nationally known as a place where African Americans could own property and enjoy leisure during an era of widespread segregation.
photo_notes: Confirmed — historic and present-day photos available.

name: Morton’s Motel
description: Morton’s Motel is a surviving example of Idlewild’s long tradition of Black travel, hospitality and community preservation. When the property faced a sale that could have removed it from its historic community purpose, a group of Idlewilders pooled resources to keep it locally connected. Today it remains a place for lodging, events, reunions and community activity.
photo_notes: Confirmed — extensive historic and current images available.

name: Robert H. Riffe Youth Center / ILOA
description: The Idlewild Lot Owners Association has helped shape community life for more than a century through civic improvement, fellowship, cultural programs and youth activities. After a donation of land and cash from the widow Margaret Riffe in 1954, the organization developed youth programming here, and the Robert H. Riffe Youth Center opened around 1962. It remains a symbol of investment in Idlewild’s next generation.
photo_notes: Documented, including preservation-plan images.

name: The Flamingo
description: Opened by Detroit hotelier Phil Giles in the 1950s, the Flamingo became one of Idlewild’s signature nightspots on Williams Island. Music, dancing and live entertainment drew visitors from across the Midwest and helped earn Idlewild its reputation as the “Summer Apollo of Michigan.” The club stood at the center of an entertainment culture created for Black audiences during segregation.
photo_notes: Confirmed — historical photographs and current remains/restoration imagery.

name: Yates School #4 / Township Hall / Festival Grounds
description: This site represents another chapter in the civic life of Idlewild: education, township government and community gathering. As Idlewild evolved beyond its resort-era peak, public spaces such as schools, halls and festival grounds became important places for residents to organize, celebrate and carry the community forward.
photo_notes: Likely available if the building/site survives or appears in township archives.

name: Hotel Casa Blanca
description: Completed in 1949, Hotel Casa Blanca was one of Idlewild’s premier accommodations. Designed and built by Woolsey Coombs and operated by Iva Lee Coombs, the Spanish Revival hotel included guest rooms and the Casbah Cocktail Lounge. Today, a preservation effort is working to rehabilitate the historic building for lodging, meetings and heritage education.
photo_notes: Confirmed — excellent historic and current restoration photos available.

name: Charles W. Chesnutt Home
description: Celebrated author, educator and civil-rights advocate Charles W. Chesnutt discovered Idlewild in 1921 and made it part of his family’s summers for years. He purchased this lakeside property in 1924, and the family cabin was completed in 1926. Chesnutt’s presence connects Idlewild to a national history of Black literature, activism and intellectual life.
photo_notes: Chesnutt family/Idlewild imagery exists.

name: Bayview / Gregory Home
description: Built by Master Electrician, Henry Gregory, Bayview tells a larger story about the arrival of modern infrastructure in a resort community growing rapidly during the early twentieth century. Electricity transformed homes, businesses and nightlife in Idlewild, allowing the community’s famous clubs and gathering places to flourish after dark.
photo_notes: Unknown — likely local archive.

name: Joseph Howard
description: Idlewild’s story is deeply connected to Detroit’s music and broadcasting communities. Joltin’ Joe Howard, a pioneering broadcaster, songwriter and recording artist whose career took him from Texas to Atlanta and ultimately to Detroit, where he became the first voice heard on one of the nation’s pioneering Black-owned radio stations.
photo_notes: Unknown — possibly available through Detroit broadcasting or family archives.

name: Tabernacle A.M.E. Church
description: Religious life has been part of Idlewild from its earliest years. H. Franklin and Virginia Bray helped establish the congregation that became Tabernacle Church, whose first rustic building was completed in 1923. Rebuilt after its roof collapsed during the winter of 1928–29, Tabernacle, the first Idlewild Church, has remained a spiritual and community institution for generations.
photo_notes: Confirmed — historical and current images available.

name: LeeJon’s Novelty Shop
description: Built in 1949 by John and Leona Simmons, LeeJon’s began as a confectionery and gift shop offering a soda bar, souvenirs and everyday goods. Places like LeeJon’s show the range of Black-owned businesses that once supported Idlewild’s thriving visitor economy — and the possibilities for reusing historic commercial spaces today.
photo_notes: Historic/current images should be findable.

name: Carrie Warner / Barbara Johnson Home
description: This home represents the extraordinary network of Black professionals and leaders who made Idlewild their summer community. Historical imagery places Carrie Warner here alongside W.E.B. Du Bois, attorney Violette Anderson and other prominent Idlewilders — a reminder that the resort was also a gathering place for Black intellectual, professional and civic life.
photo_notes: Confirmed — a particularly valuable historic image exists.

name: Black Eden Brews
description: Black Eden Brews carries Idlewild’s tradition of Black entrepreneurship into the present. Owned and operated by a fourth- and fifth-generation Idlewild family, the coffee bar brings together food, art, gifts and conversation inside historic Morton’s Motel. It is a contemporary gathering place rooted directly in the community’s multigenerational story.
photo_notes: Confirmed — extensive current imagery available.

name: Rosana’s / Red Rooster / Peyton’s & Idlewild’s Neighborhood Businesses
description: Restaurants, taverns and tea rooms were essential to everyday life in Black Eden. This site began as the Rose’s Tea Room in the early 1930’s and later became Rosanna’s Tavern, the Red Rooster and, most recently, Peyton’s Place. Its changing names tell a century-long story of Black-owned hospitality, food, music and neighborhood gathering in Idlewild.
photo_notes: Confirmed for Rosana/Red Rooster/Peyton’s; earlier names may require local archives.
